title: C strings, character arrays and the null terminator
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its output.
Identify relevant boundary and safety cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: C represents strings conventionally as arrays of char ending in the null character '\0'. A character array is not necessarily a valid string unless a terminator occurs within its accessible storage.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept supports correct handling of C data and helps prevent invalid memory access or incorrect program behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of the construct as a precisely bounded sequence of storage and operations.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, types or undefined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
C represents strings conventionally as arrays of char ending in the null character '\0'. A character array is not necessarily a valid string unless a terminator occurs within its accessible storage.

Always check the types, object bounds and preconditions required by the operation. Compile with warnings enabled and test ordinary as well as boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: The terminator tells functions such as puts and strlen where the string ends. Storage must include the terminator in addition to visible characters.

practise.guidedTask: The array contains four char elements: C, a, t and the terminating null character. Its storage size is four bytes because sizeof(char) is one byte.
practise.independentTask: Mark the element that terminates the string and predict what changes if it is removed.
hints: Create a string array with capacity for a word and its terminator; explain the required capacity.
A string literal such as "cat" includes a terminating null character.
A char array without a terminator must not be passed to functions expecting a string.
